title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside Every Segment — Products, Customers & Real-World Examples
question: What exactly does Creative sell, to whom and on what economics, and how much of the ₹2,700 Cr is consumer brand, enterprise trade, licence income or project work?

epigraph.quote: we see distribution as a strategic infrastructure, which gives us cost leverage, which gives us visibility and also gives us foot into the door.
epigraph.author: Ketan Patel, Chairman & Managing Director, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026

web_blocks.text: Creative reports two segments, Market Entry Specialist and Brand Business, and the split checks out three ways. The audited FY26 consolidated note shows Brand at ₹38,085.50 lakh (₹380.86 Cr) and Market Entry at ₹2,31,891.75 lakh (₹2,318.92 Cr) [1]. The reviewed results filed on 28 October 2026 show Q2 FY27 at ₹143.12 Cr and ₹609.02 Cr. The same filing puts H1 FY27 at ₹213.39 Cr and ₹1,014.81 Cr [10]. The Q2 FY27 investor presentation prints the same figures [2]. They agree to the rupee. The only wrinkle is a rounding difference in the Q2 FY26 Brand comparative (₹84.03 Cr in one deck, ₹84.04 Cr in the next). The split matters because Brand supplies about 14% of revenue and, on management's account, close to half of EBITDA. Market Entry is a low-margin engine whose character is easy to misread from the label [7].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated segment revenue by period (₹ Cr; Q1 to Q3 from the quarterly decks, other periods from audited or reviewed filings)
web_blocks.takeaway: Market Entry did the volume growth (it doubled in Q4 FY26). Brand's quarterly share ranges from 10% to 20% mainly because Market Entry billing is lumpy, so the annual share of 14% to 15% is the fair measure. [1][3][10]

web_blocks.text: Three readings follow. First, Market Entry carried FY26: revenue rose 54.2% for the year and doubled in the March quarter. Brand rose 40.7% for the year and fell 6.5% in that quarter [3]. Second, Brand's share is largely a residual of Market Entry's lumpiness. It reached 20.3% in Q4 FY25 when Market Entry was weak (₹321.13 Cr), 19.0% in Q2 FY27 in the festive-stocking quarter, and only 10.3% in Q4 FY26 when Market Entry doubled. A single quarter therefore says little [2][3]. Third, Q2 FY27 is the quarter management wants: Brand up 70.3% to ₹143.12 Cr against Market Entry up 6.7% [10]. Part of that jump is WOZOYO, the owned brand, which management says sold close to $2.2 million (about ₹20 Cr) in its first months in the United States [4]. If that sat inside Q2, Brand revenue excluding WOZOYO grew about 46%, our arithmetic because the segment note does not split WOZOYO out. Management's FY27 aim of ₹475 Cr to ₹500 Cr for Honeywell plus WOZOYO implies H2 FY27 Brand revenue of ₹262 Cr to ₹287 Cr against ₹232.09 Cr in H2 FY26. That is a rise of 13% to 23% [4][2][3].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated segment results (₹ Cr; segment result is revenue less allocable cost, before finance cost and unallocable cost)
web_blocks.takeaway: Brand earns a segment margin of 33% to 36% and has not moved. The change in H1 FY27 is Market Entry, whose result margin doubled from 3.4% to 6.7% on revenue up only 12.9%. [1][10]

web_blocks.text: Segment results flatter both segments because they stop before overhead. In FY26 the two results totalled ₹213.58 Cr. Finance cost of ₹20.66 Cr and 'unallocable cost' of ₹111.15 Cr (4.1% of revenue) take that to the ₹81.76 Cr pre-tax profit [1][3]. So the 3.8% Market Entry margin is before its share of staff, marketing and administration. A cleaner cut uses management's own claim that Brand earns an EBITDA margin of about 13% [5]. On ₹380.86 Cr that is roughly ₹49.5 Cr. That leaves about ₹54.4 Cr of the ₹103.95 Cr group EBITDA for Market Entry, or 2.3% of its revenue. That is our estimate, and it squares with the CFO's agreement in November 2025 that Brand supplies roughly half of EBITDA [7]. The H1 FY27 jump in Market Entry profitability is real in the filings. Management attributes it to gross profit in Market Entry rising by close to 200 basis points, and the consolidated gross margin was 11.34% in Q2 FY27 against 7.90% a year earlier [4][2]. The same measure was 9.41% against 11.54% in Q4 FY26, so gross margin swings between roughly 8% and 11.5% by quarter on product mix [3]. We would not extrapolate one quarter.

web_blocks.title: What is inside Market Entry: mostly enterprise trade

web_blocks.text: The Market Entry label suggests brand distribution. The older four-way segment disclosure says otherwise. In FY25 the audited notes showed Enterprise Business (EB) at ₹1,205.95 Cr, FMCT (fast-moving consumer technology) at ₹182.04 Cr. They put FMEG at ₹1.12 Cr and FMSG (fast-moving social-media gadgets, the home of Honeywell) at ₹385.36 Cr (AR FY25). Take out the ₹270.68 Cr that later became the Brand segment, and the remainder of FMSG is ₹114.68 Cr. If the whole Brand segment sat inside FMSG, the FY25 Market Entry segment of ₹1,503.80 Cr reconstructs as EB ₹1,205.95 Cr plus FMCT ₹182.04 Cr plus other FMSG ₹114.68 Cr plus FMEG ₹1.12 Cr [1]. About 80% of Market Entry in FY25 was therefore the enterprise trade. The FY26 report dropped the old split, so the current mix is not published. The reconstruction is our inference, but Crisil's description of customer concentration is consistent with it [13]. Management describes the trade in plain words: 'it is basically back-to-back business, which you sell to large corporates' (Q1 FY24 call). It earned a gross margin of 2.09% in FY25 and 2.61% in FY24 [6], against 6% to 7% for the channel business [7].

web_blocks.title: Geography: where the revenue is billed

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated revenue by place of billing (₹ Cr; sale of products)
rows: Enterprise trade begins to scale (AR FY23)
web_blocks.takeaway: Until FY25 most revenue was billed outside India; in FY26 two-thirds is billed in India, and the swing is the whole of the FY26 growth. [1]

web_blocks.text: The FY23 annual report prints a different and apparently transposed FY23 split (India ₹850.20 Cr, outside ₹526.02 Cr). The table uses the restated comparative in the FY24 report because it matches management's own comment that about ₹875 Cr of FY23 revenue was foreign [8]. Two derived numbers sharpen the picture. The parent's own overseas billing was ₹754.03 Cr in FY26 against ₹960.14 Cr in FY25. The parent's Brand segment (₹232.24 Cr) is almost exactly Honeywell India (₹231.98 Cr), so nearly all of that overseas billing is Market Entry exports [1][5]. On that basis exports were about 33% of Market Entry in FY26 and about 64% in FY25. The filings do not name the buyers. Crisil says the largest customer is now about 25% of revenue against a historical 50% to 60% and sets a downgrade trigger at 40% [13]. The historical range is close to the overseas share of revenue in FY24 and FY25, so a large overseas trading counterparty is the likeliest identity. That is inference, not disclosure.

Brand geography is disclosed more cleanly. Honeywell sold ₹231.98 Cr in India and ₹137.6 Cr outside in FY26, ₹369.61 Cr in all [5]. A year earlier it was ₹133 Cr in India and ₹121 Cr outside (Q4 FY25 call), so India grew 74% and overseas 14%. Overseas splits roughly evenly between South-East Asia and the Middle East. Management warned in May 2026 that Middle East sales could halve while Red Sea shipping stayed disrupted [5]. The licence territory is described inconsistently. The count was 29 countries in 2022, 38 in 2023 and in the FY26 report, 37 by the CFO in May 2025, 'close to 40' and '42' by the chairman in November 2025, and 'over 29' in the Q2 FY27 management biography [1][2][6][7] (Q4 FY22 call). Operating presence was at least 13 countries in November 2025 [7]. Our reconciliation: 38 is the only count printed in the annual reports (FY23 and FY26) and is the figure used in this report. The figure 29 is the FY22 mandate and the Secure Connection chief executive's biography, while 37, 'close to 40' and 42 are remarks on calls. The FY26 notice of meeting describes the licence territory as Hong Kong, South-East Asia and the Pacific. The chairman instead names South-East Asia, South Asia, the Middle East and Africa [1][7]. Licence rights are not operating presence. Creative holds no Honeywell rights in the United States or Europe, which is why WOZOYO exists [5].

Channel mix is described but not quantified. The annual report lists general trade, large-format retail, e-commerce, quick commerce, direct-to-consumer websites and the government e-marketplace as routes to market. Honeywell listed directly on Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in FY26 [1]. The chairman says only 8% to 10% of Indian consumer electronics is sold online against 80% to 90% offline. He adds that the Middle East is nearly all modern retail with online at about 2%, and that Indonesia sells through TikTok live commerce [7]. Honeywell reached 450 Nesto stores in Saudi Arabia in 2025 and chains such as Lulu and Saraf DG in Dubai [6]. Quick-commerce sales grew more than 100% across India, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in FY26 [5]. Listing is a fixed cost: Honeywell paid AED 450,000 to AED 500,000 a year in listing fees at Gulf power-retail chains (Q4 FY23 call). No filing splits revenue by channel, so the mix cannot be stated. The qualitative picture is a business that earns its Indian volume in offline and enterprise channels and its brand margin online.

web_blocks.takeaway: Twelve lines, but three carry the money: enterprise trade supplies volume, Honeywell supplies profit, and Make-in-India surveillance and compute supply the growth that cost working capital in FY26. [1][5][6]

web_blocks.text: The map says more about risk than about size. The largest line by revenue earns about 2% gross margin and depends on a few counterparties. The highest-margin line is about 97% of Brand revenue. That is the CFO's ₹369.61 Cr, given in reply to a question on Honeywell, against the audited ₹380.86 Cr segment, and the ₹11 Cr gap is other brands. The line sits on a single licence that management says is due for renewal in March 2027 [5]. The growth lines are small, new and unproven in the numbers: no filing gives revenue for surveillance, drones, servers or government work beyond the order values quoted. That is the honest position for an investor today. Management's own FY29 plan wants Brand at 40% of ₹6,000 Cr. That means the unproven lines, the licences and WOZOYO have to be much larger than anything the company has yet reported [2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Only the Honeywell and CyberPower arrangements give Creative something it owns or controls for years. Most other partnerships are distribution rights a vendor can narrow, as the Samsung state count shows. [1][5]

web_blocks.text: Territorial rights are the currency of this business and they are not permanent. Samsung's monitor territory shrank from 22 states to 16 or 17 between August 2023 and October 2024. Management accepts churn as policy. Brands are expected to stay 8 to 10 years, but a board mandate in 2023 was to drop four or five brands that failed the return test (Q4 FY23 call). The stated aim is that 30% to 35% of sales should come from brands under three years old [8]. The company's internal test is a return on capital employed of 20% to 22% on each brand [7]. For an investor, the implication is that revenue in the distribution book has to be re-earned continuously through new vendors. That is exactly what FY26 shows. Exclusivity statements in decks should also be read against the releases, which are more cautious. Brand counts are inconsistent too: 'over 20' in the media-release boilerplate, '26+' in the annual report and '50+' in the investor decks [1][2].

The annual report gives no top-customer or top-vendor table, so concentration has to be pieced together. Customers: Crisil puts the largest customer at about 25% of FY26 revenue, down from a historical 50% to 60% [13]. Channel breadth is wide, with 10,000-plus trusted partners, 31-plus branches and 2,305 pin codes served [1]. Related-party customers are small. Click Retail (₹26.78 Cr), World EMS (₹26.70 Cr) and a handful of others total about ₹58.6 Cr, or 2.2% of consolidated revenue, excluding sales to the group's own Hong Kong subsidiary [1]. The one related-party balance that matters is Click Retail's ₹47.74 Cr outstanding balance at March 2026, equal to 8.4% of consolidated trade receivables. The schedule does not break it into trade and advances [1]. Vendors: the annual report lists about 30 vendors by category without volumes [1]. Dependence is highest on Honeywell, which is about 97% of Brand revenue. It is also high on Indian OEMs in surveillance and compute, many of them small suppliers who give little credit. That is why borrowings at March 2026 included ₹171.19 Cr of TReDS supplier finance used to pay MSME vendors within 45 days [3]. Purchases from the group's own Hong Kong subsidiary were ₹155.39 Cr in FY26 [1].

The operating base is thin. The group had 355 employees at 31 March 2026 (the MD&A says 'over 350'), of whom 202 were permanent staff on the parent's own rolls [1]. It runs 18 pan-India warehouses with over 125,000 sq ft and a Bhiwandi mother warehouse authorised as a private bonded warehouse. It also runs 18-plus global warehouses including mainland China and Dubai, with more than 2,000 cubic metres of capacity [1]. FY26 volumes were 533 import containers and 55,453 domestic transactions [1]. Consolidated employee cost was ₹21.30 Cr, 0.8% of revenue from operations, and revenue per group employee was about ₹7.6 Cr [3][1]. Fixed assets were only ₹12 Cr against total assets of ₹937 Cr at March 2026 [12]. Management says logistics costs about 1.1% of sales and that it operates through 14 stocking points and 28 locations (Q2 FY25 call). The asset-light model is why the balance sheet is a working-capital ledger. It is also why employee cost rose 73% in H1 FY27 (₹15.99 Cr against ₹9.26 Cr) as the company hired people who understand servers, surveillance and AI [2][5].

web_blocks.company: ASBISc Enterprises Plc (Cyprus; listed in Warsaw)
web_blocks.region_era: Central and Eastern Europe, CIS, Middle East and Africa; 1990 to 2025
web_blocks.mechanism: An emerging-market IT distributor uses a thin-margin distribution book (smartphones, components, servers) to fund and feed private-label brands. Far East OEMs make those brands (Canyon, Prestigio Solutions, AENO, Lorgar), and they are sold through the same customers. It is the same distribution-to-owned-brand ladder Creative is climbing, now with a swing into AI servers.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: It started in 1990 distributing Seagate products in the CIS. 2025 revenue was US$3,862,999 thousand, up 28.4% from US$3,008,503 thousand. Gross margin fell to 7.22% from 7.98%. Net profit was US$60.2 million, up 11.2%. Servers and server blocks were US$698.8 million against US$254.7 million. The largest customer was 5.0% of revenue. It has about 20,000 customers in about 60 countries. Research and development came to US$1.1 million behind four own brands.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: ASBIS scaled revenue through the distribution book and a server boom. Its directors still call own brands a reinforcement 'if they are developed as an addition to the distribution business', and blended gross margin stayed in single digits after three decades. Creative's plan for a 40% Brand share by FY29 is far more aggressive than that outcome. Its FY26 surge was component- and server-led in the same way, so gross margin and cash conversion are the metrics to watch rather than headline growth. [14]

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 1: Market-entry distribution of an experiential brand (Cricut and Razer)
paragraphs: Customer and problem. Cricut makes connected cutting machines that let hobbyists cut, emboss and print on dozens of materials; Razer makes premium gaming peripherals. Neither had an India organisation. Creative signed distribution for Cricut on 10 April 2023 and for all Razer products on 5 May 2023 (Cricut release; Razer release). The buyers are Indian crafters and gamers, reached through Amazon, retailers and influencers.

What is bought and how it is priced. A shopper buys, for example, a Cricut Joy machine. Creative buys the machine in bulk from Cricut on its own account (principal-to-principal). It sells the machine to Amazon or a retailer at a discount to the list price and keeps the spread. The channel business earned a gross margin of 8.5% to 8.7% in 2023 and 6% to 7% in H1 FY26 [7] (Q1 FY24 call). Marketing is largely paid by the brand. The then CFO said brand and promotion spend is 'always passed through' and is included in gross margin [8], so reported gross margin overstates the pure spread. For brands other than Honeywell the company says it pays nothing from its own pocket for marketing [8].

How it is built, shipped, billed and collected. Imports clear through the Bhiwandi bonded warehouse [1]. The first Cricut launch was on Amazon Prime Day 2023 and sold about ₹55 lakh of product in two days. Creative then ran four to five influencer demonstrations a month, 60 to 70 a year, in Mumbai, Delhi and Bangalore (Q1 FY24 call). Channel debtors run about 40 days and logistics costs about 1.1% of sales (Q2 FY25 call).

What Creative earns. On every ₹100 of sales Creative keeps a gross spread of about ₹6 to ₹9. After logistics and selling cost, the parent's EBITDA margin on the whole distribution business was 2.58% in H1 FY26 [7]. Our estimate for a mature brand like this is a 2.5% to 3% EBITDA margin on sales. We also estimate a return on capital employed near the 20% to 22% hurdle the board applies [7]. The economics are modest per rupee of sale; the value to Creative is the foot in the door with retailers that its own brands later use.

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 2: Honeywell licensing and contract manufacturing
paragraphs: Customer and problem. A Delhi household orders a Honeywell air purifier through Blinkit, or a Dubai household buys one on Amazon. The shopper wants a trusted name in a category with few incumbents. Creative's answer is the Honeywell brand on a product Creative designed. Honeywell air purifiers reached number one on Amazon UAE and the top three on Amazon India. The company says it sold one Honeywell product every 60 seconds online in FY26 [1][5].

What is bought and how it is priced. The product is one of four categories. Air purifiers were about ₹79 Cr of ₹255 Cr in FY25, IT accessories ₹84 Cr, audio ₹50 Cr and structured cabling ₹41 Cr [6]. Creative decides the price: 'We can decide the price that we will sell the product' (Q1 FY24 call). Honeywell is paid the greater of a minimum guarantee or a percentage of sales (same call). Gross margin is about 40% to 42% on the latest management figure [4], against 35% to 36% in FY25 (Q2 FY25 call).

How it is built, shipped, billed and collected. The product is built by contract factories in China, Taiwan and India (about 28 facilities). Honeywell audits the factory and approves the design and packaging [1][6]. Certification such as BIS costs about ₹2 lakh a product and takes about seven months in India [7][6]. Secure Connection in Hong Kong buys from the factory and sells to distributors such as Trigon in the UAE (Trigon release). It also sells to the Indian parent, which bought ₹155.39 Cr in FY26 [1]. Honeywell's working capital ran about 60 days against 40 to 45 for other brands in 2023 [8]. Q3 is the peak season for purifiers and audio.

What Creative earns. Per ₹100 of Honeywell sales, gross profit is about ₹40 to ₹42 and marketing about ₹9 (₹32 Cr to ₹33 Cr on ₹369.61 Cr in FY26 [5]). Manpower is about ₹6 to ₹7 [5], leaving an EBITDA of about ₹13 [5]. That leaves roughly ₹12 for royalty, freight, certification and other overheads. The audited notes carry a royalty expense line of only ₹5.96 Cr, 1.6% of Honeywell sales [1]. The note does not name Honeywell as the payee, so we treat it as the likely licence charge rather than a confirmed one. The profit sits in Hong Kong. The parent's own Brand segment earns ₹24.53 Cr on ₹232.24 Cr (10.6%), while the consolidated Brand segment earns ₹126.29 Cr on ₹380.86 Cr (33.2%). The subsidiary therefore earns about ₹101.8 Cr of segment result before overhead, and 22.5% of the subsidiary's profit belongs to its chief executive [1].

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 3: Enterprise and government orders (FCI, BSNL and the other releases)
paragraphs: FCI: what is established. Creative announced on 12 May 2026 a ₹35.89 Cr 'order from the Food Corporation of India' for smart warehousing across 150 depots. The order comes in two phases of 75 sites, with commissioning within 180 days and three years of maintenance. The scope covers sensor modules, bag counting, boom barriers, gateways, software, surveillance and AI monitoring (release). After the exchange sought format details, an addendum on 13 May confirmed the numbers (addendum). On 11 September 2026 the company clarified that FCI awarded the project to its systems-integrator partner NebulArc Technologies. Creative's order for its assigned scope came from NebulArc, which is the direct counterparty [11].

FCI: what is not established. The filings do not say what share of NebulArc's FCI contract Creative holds, the margin, or the payment terms. The original headline implied a direct FCI order. The clarification shows it is a sub-contract; the promoter has no interest in NebulArc, and it is not a related party [11]. Our estimate is a gross margin of 8% to 12%, or ₹3 Cr to ₹4 Cr of gross profit over about 180 days plus the maintenance tail. It rests on management's remark that Indian-made supply earns a higher percentage than the 6% to 7% channel margin [5][7]. This is a small order against ₹2,700 Cr of revenue; its value is the credential.

BSNL: what is established. On 6 June 2026 Creative, 'along with its consortium partner', received an Advance Work Order from BSNL, acting for Digital Bharat Nidhi, for the BharatNet Middle Mile Network in the Odisha circle. The quoted 'total all-inclusive AWO value for the consortium is approximately INR 3,194.83 crore' covers design, supply, construction, installation, upgradation, operation and maintenance over about three years. The order is subject to unconditional acceptance, performance security, an executed agreement and route-wise work orders [11]. Crisil describes the group as project implementation agency for the circle [13].

BSNL: what is not established. Creative's share of the consortium, the partner's name and the performance-security size are undisclosed. On the October 2026 call management split the work into about ₹1,700 Cr of capital spending and ₹1,200 Cr of seven-year operation and maintenance. It guided to billing of ₹150 Cr to ₹200 Cr in Q4 FY27 and ₹500 Cr to ₹600 Cr next year. It also said 'you can expect net profit out of that close to 6% to 7% of the value we bill' [4]. The two parts total ₹2,900 Cr against the ₹3,194.83 Cr headline, a gap the call does not explain. At 6% to 7% the profit would be ₹9 Cr to ₹14 Cr in FY27 and ₹30 Cr to ₹42 Cr in FY28. Because that is two to three times the group's 2.6% PAT margin, we would use a central 4%, or ₹6 Cr to ₹8 Cr in FY27. Two other releases are not orders at all. The 27 October 2026 'award' is an Amazon Ads recognition for WOZOYO (release). The 12 November 2026 AT&T release is a brand licence with no revenue or minimum disclosed (release). The Zicom SaaS release is an acquisition of a subscription-monitoring business with ₹20.09 Cr of FY26 revenue and a net worth of ₹25.62 Cr. The enterprise value is ₹50.50 Cr (board outcome).

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 4: Surveillance and new technology (Sparsh, Matrix, Infinova, drones)
paragraphs: Customer and problem. A state agency or a systems integrator needs CCTV that meets the government's STQC security certification. The certification requires that no component originates in China, that the software and board design files are made in India, and that no director or beneficiary of the maker is Chinese [4]. Matrix and Sparsh are two of the four Indian STQC-certified makers; Creative became their pan-India distributor in November 2025 (Matrix; Sparsh).

What is bought and how it is priced. The integrator buys cameras, recorders and software from Creative at a distributor price. Management says these small Indian makers carry a higher percentage margin than larger vendors but give less credit. Creative therefore pays earlier and carries more receivables. The FY26 deck says 'vendor credit remains limited, resulting in higher advance payments' [5][3]. Revenue from Matrix and Sparsh is not disclosed; the makers' own turnovers were about ₹250 Cr and ₹400 Cr in FY25, according to the chairman [7].

How the build-out works. Creative is buying Infinova (India) Pvt Ltd, a Pune assembler of high-end cameras used in smart cities and airports. The deal comes with a board budget of up to USD 4.00 Million, exclusive India brand rights and its own small factory (release). Infinova's revenue fell from ₹38 Cr to ₹32 Cr last March for lack of STQC. Management's goalpost is ₹75 Cr to ₹80 Cr in the first full year and ₹200 Cr in the next, and 'the crucial number is to do INR75 crores' [4]. On drones, Creative distributes PDRL, Drona Aviation's STEM kits and Jupiter's BIS-certified 24,000 mAh agricultural-drone battery, with no volumes disclosed.

What it means. Surveillance is the best-fitting adjacency, because the same integrators buy Honeywell cabling, and ownership of Infinova would move part of it into the Brand segment. The chairman suggests surveillance 'can easily' reach ₹2,000 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr in two to three years [4]. We regard that as well beyond what the evidence supports, since the only quantified base is Infinova at ₹32 Cr and the target year-one number is ₹75 Cr to ₹80 Cr.

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 5: WOZOYO, the owned brand on Amazon
paragraphs: Customer and problem. A US shopper wants an air purifier or a laptop docking station at an affordable-premium price. Creative cannot sell Honeywell air purifiers in the United States, where the category is about ₹28,000 Cr against about ₹2,000 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr in India. It therefore created WOZOYO under Secure Connection, announced on 15 June 2026 and sold in the United States from the end of July [4] (release).

What is bought and how it is priced. The product is built by the same contract manufacturers that serve Honeywell, sold on Amazon, TikTok and later Walmart and Best Buy. Management's strategy is 'build online trust and credibility' first [4]. In India, quick-commerce platforms usually want sale-or-return from new brands; the chairman says WOZOYO accepts none, even at the cost of sales [4]. The target gross margin is 37% to 40% [4].

How it is built, shipped, billed and collected. Inventory was already in Amazon's US warehouses before the May 2026 launch [5]. The company reports about $2.2 million (roughly ₹20 Cr) sold in the first months and returns of about 3% to 3.5% against 8% to 9% typical. It also reports an Amazon's Choice badge for the docking station and an Amazon Ads 'New Rising Star' award [4]. The launch window is end July to end September, which is two months of selling, although the chairman describes it as three.

What Creative earns. Today, little. Amazon marketing services run at about 50% of sales, falling to 12% to 14% once sales reach about $1 million. The company has spent about ₹12 Cr of a ₹20 Cr to ₹22 Cr brand-building budget [4]. Against a 37% to 40% gross margin, 50% advertising means a negative contribution (about −₹10 to −₹13 per ₹100 of sales before other costs, our arithmetic). At 12% to 14% it turns positive at about ₹23 to ₹28. The FY27 target is ₹45 Cr to ₹50 Cr, the next year ₹100 Cr to ₹150 Cr. Because WOZOYO sits in Secure Connection, 22.5% of its profit or loss belongs to the subsidiary's chief executive. Management calls Secure Connection 'wholly owned' on the Q2 FY27 call, but the annual report shows 77.50%, which is the figure used here [4][1].

web_blocks.text: Put together, the business is four things under one roof. A low-margin enterprise trade that moves ₹1,000 Cr-plus a year on little capital in good years and a lot of credit in bad ones. A channel distribution book that pays for the national infrastructure and gives access to retailers. A licence business, Honeywell, that earns the profit and sits offshore. And a set of new bets in surveillance, compute, drones and owned brands whose revenue is not yet visible in the segment note. FY26 grew because the first and fourth were enlarged together; H1 FY27 earned more because Market Entry's margin widened and Brand grew 43%. Whether the margin gain and the working-capital release last is the question the next chapters take up.

book_paragraphs: Let me give you the ledger first and the stories second. Creative reports two segments. Market Entry Specialist made ₹2,318.92 Cr of revenue in FY26 and Brand Business made ₹380.86 Cr. In the half-year to September 2026 the numbers were ₹1,014.81 Cr and ₹213.39 Cr. I checked those against the audited note, the reviewed results and the investor presentation, and they agree to the rupee. Brand is about 14% of the revenue and, on management's own account, close to half of the EBITDA. If you remember only one thing from this chapter, remember that gap: a segment that is one-seventh of sales produces roughly half of the profit, and the other six-sevenths earn their living on very thin spreads. Keep the labels in view as we go: Market Entry, Brand, order, award, licence. Each one hides a precise legal meaning, and the money behind them differs enormously.

Now open the larger segment, because its label is misleading. 'Market Entry' sounds like a company ushering foreign brands into India. In FY25, when the older four-way split was still published, about 80% of it was something else: the enterprise business, ₹1,205.95 Cr of it. Ketan Patel has described it simply: 'it is basically back-to-back business, which you sell to large corporates.' Gross margin was 2.09% in FY25. Think of a trader who takes an order from a buyer, places the matching order with a supplier, and keeps two paise on the rupee for arranging it. The business needs almost no warehouse, but it needs trust, and it needs credit when the buyer is slow. It is also the line that has swung most. In FY24 about 73% of group revenue was billed outside India, and in FY26 it was 33%. I mention it now because the rest of the chapter keeps returning to that two-paise margin.

That geographic swing is the single most useful fact in the chapter. India-billed revenue was ₹678 Cr in FY25 and ₹1,797 Cr in FY26. Billing outside India fell from ₹1,096 Cr to ₹903 Cr. The parent company's own overseas billing, which is almost all Market Entry exports, was about ₹960 Cr in FY25 and ₹754 Cr in FY26. Crisil says the largest customer was 25% of revenue in FY26 against 50 to 60% historically. The filings do not name that customer, so I will only say what I would say to a colleague: the size of the old concentration matches the size of the overseas book, and one large buyer has been replaced, in part, by a larger number of Indian buyers. That is a good change for risk, and a costly one for working capital.

Before the first walkthrough, a word on channels, because 'distribution' hides how the goods actually reach people. The annual report lists general trade, large-format retail, e-commerce, quick commerce, direct-to-consumer websites and the government e-marketplace. In India, the chairman says, only 8 to 10% of consumer electronics is sold online and 80 to 90% is offline, although quick commerce is eating into both. In the Middle East it is nearly all modern retail, with online at about 2%. Honeywell is in 450 Nesto stores in Saudi Arabia and in Lulu and Saraf DG in Dubai, and it sold over 100% more through quick commerce in India, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in FY26. Retail listing is a fixed cost: Honeywell paid AED 450,000 to AED 500,000 a year for listing fees at chains in the Gulf. No channel revenue split is published, so this is the picture, not the accounting.

Let me take you to a stall in the first walkthrough. You are a crafter looking at a Cricut Joy on Amazon on Prime Day 2023. Behind that listing, Creative signed a distribution agreement in April 2023 and imported the machines through its Bhiwandi bonded warehouse. It sold about ₹55 lakh of product in two days, then ran 60 to 70 influencer demonstrations a year in Mumbai, Delhi and Bangalore. Creative buys on its own account and keeps a gross spread of roughly 6 to 9%, depending on the year. After logistics at about 1.1% of sales and selling cost, the parent's EBITDA margin on the whole distribution business was 2.58% in H1 FY26. The CFO once explained that brand-funded marketing is 'always passed through' and included in gross margin. So the headline spread is a little richer than the true one. The foot in the door is the point.

The second walkthrough is where the profit lives. A Delhi household orders a Honeywell air purifier on Blinkit. Honeywell does not make it. Creative designed it, a contract factory in China built it after Honeywell audited the plant, and a Hong Kong subsidiary, Secure Connection, bought it and sold it on. Ketan Patel is explicit about who sets the price: 'We can decide the price that we will sell the product.' Honeywell gets the greater of a minimum guarantee or a percentage of sales. Gross margin is about 40 to 42%, marketing about 9% of sales, manpower 6 to 7%, and EBITDA about 13%. The residual of roughly 12 points must cover the royalty, freight and certification. The audited notes show a royalty expense of only ₹5.96 Cr, about 1.6% of Honeywell sales, which I take to be the licence charge although the note does not name the payee.

Here is a detail that shows where the margin sits. In the parent company's books, the Honeywell business in India earns a segment result of ₹24.53 Cr on ₹232.24 Cr of sales, 10.6%. In the consolidated books the Brand segment earns ₹126.29 Cr on ₹380.86 Cr, 33.2%. The difference is the margin captured by Secure Connection, which is 77.5% owned. Its chief executive, Mohit Anand, owns the remaining 22.5%, so ₹8.42 Cr of FY26 consolidated profit belonged to minority holders. I find this structure sensible and common, but I want you to see it: when you hear 'Brand earns 33%', the cash that comes up to Creative's shareholders is smaller, because Hong Kong keeps a share and the royalty line in the notes, at ₹5.96 Cr, is small enough to deserve a question about how it is set.

The third walkthrough is the one I most want you to read carefully, because the headlines can mislead. In May 2026 the company announced a ₹35.89 Cr order 'from the Food Corporation of India' for smart warehousing at 150 depots. In September, after an exchange query and an addendum, it clarified that FCI had awarded the project to a systems integrator called NebulArc, and that Creative's order came from NebulArc for its assigned scope. That is a sub-contract. It is established that the value is ₹35.89 Cr, the sites are 150, the commissioning window is 180 days and maintenance runs three years. It is not established what Creative's margin is. My estimate is 8 to 12% gross, or ₹3 to ₹4 Cr, which tells you the order is a credential and not an earnings event.

BSNL is the same lesson at a hundred times the scale. The advance work order, announced on 6 June 2026, carries a consortium value of about ₹3,194.83 Cr for design, supply, construction and maintenance of BharatNet's Odisha middle mile. It is conditional on acceptance, performance security, an executed agreement and route-wise work orders. Creative's share is not disclosed. On the October call the chairman said 'you can expect net profit out of that close to 6% to 7% of the value we bill', and guided to ₹150 to ₹200 Cr of billing in the March 2027 quarter. At 6 to 7% that is real money, but it is two to three times the group's 2.6% PAT margin, so I would plan on 4% and treat everything above as a bonus. Two other releases that look like orders are not: one is an Amazon advertising award and one is a brand licence from AT&T.

The fourth walkthrough is surveillance. An integrator bidding for a state project needs cameras that meet the STQC rules. Ketan Patel spelled out three conditions on the call: no components sourced from China, software and board files made in India, and 'none of the directors or beneficiaries can be of Chinese nationals or Chinese citizens.' Matrix and Sparsh qualify, and Creative distributes both. Infinova, which Creative is buying for up to USD 4.00 Million, lacks STQC today because of its foreign ownership, and management says Indian ownership after closing cures the third condition. Management's goalpost is simple: 'the crucial number is to do INR75 crores' in the first full year, against ₹32 Cr last year. I like the logic, because the same integrators buy Honeywell cabling. I do not accept the chairman's claim that surveillance can reach ₹2,000 to ₹3,000 Cr in three years; the evidence supports a first rung, not the ladder.

The fifth walkthrough is the most honest one the company has given. WOZOYO, the owned brand, launched in the United States at the end of July 2026 because Creative cannot sell Honeywell air purifiers there. Ketan Patel's strategy is 'build online trust and credibility', first on Amazon and TikTok, then in stores. In the first period it sold close to $2.2 million, about ₹20 Cr, with returns of 3 to 3.5% against 8 to 9% typical. The price of that start is advertising at about half of sales, falling to 12 to 14% once sales reach about a million dollars. Against a gross margin target of 37 to 40%, the early contribution is negative; at scale it is strongly positive. The company has spent about ₹12 Cr of a ₹20 to ₹22 Cr budget. This is a bet with a clear cost and a measurable exit.

Who buys, and who supplies? The annual report gives no top-customer table, so I patched one together. Crisil says the largest customer is about 25% of revenue, with a downgrade trigger at 40%. The channel is broad, with more than 10,000 trusted partners, 31 branches and 2,305 pin codes. Related-party customers total about ₹58.6 Cr, 2.2% of revenue, though one of them, Click Retail, carried a ₹47.74 Cr outstanding balance at the year-end, equal to 8.4% of trade receivables. On the vendor side the dependence is on one licence, Honeywell, which is about 97% of Brand revenue, and on small Indian makers who give little credit. That is why borrowings include ₹171.19 Cr of TReDS finance used to pay MSME vendors inside 45 days. When your suppliers are small and your customers are the government, someone must fund the gap, and today it is the balance sheet. I would rather you hold that uncertainty than assume the concentration is gone.

Look at what carries all this: 355 employees across the group, 202 of them permanent on the parent's rolls, 18 warehouses with 125,000 square feet, a bonded warehouse in Bhiwandi and fixed assets of ₹12 Cr against ₹937 Cr of total assets. Revenue per group employee is about ₹7.6 Cr. Employee cost was ₹21.30 Cr in FY26, 0.8% of revenue. This is an asset-light business whose only real asset is the working-capital ledger, and that is why the balance sheet moves so violently when the mix changes. It also explains why employee cost jumped 73% in H1 FY27, to ₹15.99 Cr from ₹9.26 Cr: the company is hiring people who understand servers, surveillance and AI, in the chairman's words 'similar kind of skill sets we also got into the company.' Hiring ahead of revenue is a cost today and a capability later. I would watch whether employee cost stays under 1% of sales, and whether the revenue per head holds as the new teams ramp.

There is a useful outside comparison. ASBIS, a Cyprus-based distributor founded in 1990 that serves Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa, did US$3.86 billion of revenue in 2025 with a gross margin of 7.22%, down from 7.98%, and runs four own brands in the same spirit as Creative. Its servers business jumped from US$255 million to US$699 million in a year, rather like Creative's FY26 surge in India. After 35 years its directors still describe own brands as an addition to the distribution business, and the blended margin remains single-digit. I take two lessons: the distribution book can scale a long way, and owned brands lift margin slowly. Creative's plan to be 40% brand by FY29 is far more ambitious than what ASBIS has achieved. Treat it as a base rate, not a verdict.

So here is how I would summarise the business to a colleague. It has four engines. An enterprise trade that moves large volumes at two paise on the rupee and swings with cash. A channel book that pays for the infrastructure and opens doors. A licence business, Honeywell, that earns the money from a single renewable contract, and sits offshore with a minority partner. And a set of new bets in surveillance, compute, drones and own brands whose revenue is still invisible in the segment note. FY26 added the fourth engine's early invoices and a lot of the first. In H1 FY27 the margin improved, Brand grew 43%, and cash flow turned. Your job is to ask which of those improvements is durable and which is timing. Everything in the next chapters, from margins to cash conversion to risk, is a test of that question.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A company's own labels deserve the same scepticism as any headline. 'Market Entry' is mostly enterprise trade, 'order from FCI' is a sub-contract, and 'brand margin of 33%' is a segment result before overhead and before the minority partner's share. None of this is dishonest, because every fact sits in a filing. It does mean the story that reaches investors is one notch rosier than the story in the notes, and the analyst's job is to read the notes.

book_callouts.title: WHAT IS ESTABLISHED, WHAT IS IMPLIED, WHAT IS ESTIMATED
book_callouts.text: For every order or partnership announced, sort what you read into three bins: what the document states (value, scope, counterparty), what it implies but does not state (margin, share, payment terms), and what you estimate and why. Here, FCI's value is established, its margin is implied by management's talk of higher percentage margins, and our 8% to 12% is an estimate. Keeping the bins apart prevents a press release from becoming a forecast.
